docs.title: DevOps for SAS
docs.text:
Build, test, document and deploy SAS applications on Viya, SAS 9 and desktop SAS - from git, in the IDE you already use.

Get started Why SASjs

npm i -g @sasjs/cli

docs.title: The short version
docs.text:
SAS code usually lives outside the tooling everything else lives in: no repository, no tests, no build, no deploy, and a copy-paste into a stored process or a Viya job when it is ready. SASjs gives a SAS project the same shape as any other software project.

  • One project, any SAS. Compile and deploy the same services to Viya, to SAS 9 (EBI or Foundation), and to SASjs Server - the platform is a target, not a rewrite.
  • Git is the source of truth. Your code lives in a repository, not in SASAUTOS on a server whose filesystem nobody can see.
  • Test before you ship. Services are called from a test harness that runs anywhere, including CI, and coverage is measured.
  • Deploy in seconds. sasjs cbd compiles the project, builds the deployable artefact, and loads it into the target environment.
  • Documentation comes out of the code. Doxygen headers on your macros and services become a browsable site.
  • Apps, not just programs. The adapter and the CLI build and deploy HTML5 applications on SAS, with a SAS (or JS, or Python) backend.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Six pieces, usable on their own or together. What each one does.

  • CLI

    Compile, build, deploy, test and document a SAS project from the terminal or a pipeline.

    @sasjs/cli

  • Macro Core

    A library of SAS macros for application development - the runtime half of the framework.

    @sasjs/core

  • Adapter

    The JavaScript library that connects a browser or Node app to SAS, on Viya, SAS 9 or server.

    @sasjs/adapter

  • Server

    An open-source web server on Foundation SAS: a REST API, a drive, and an app portal.

    @sasjs/server

  • Lint

    Configurable SAS code-quality rules, so a style argument is settled once, in a config file.

    @sasjs/lint

  • VS Code

    Syntax highlighting, linting, execution and compile/build/deploy inside the editor.

    SASjs for VS Code

docs.title: Where it runs
docs.text:
SASjs does not need a particular SAS product to exist - it needs a place to deploy to.

Platform What deployment means SAS Viya Services become job definitions in a folder, or a web app served from a folder, in a context you choose. SAS 9 (EBI or Foundation) Services become stored processes and files under a metadata folder, deployed over the SASjs web service (ms_server). SASjs Server Services become files on the server's drive, run on SAS, JS, Python or R, with a REST API in front. Desktop SAS The same project runs against a local SAS session, which is how most development and testing is done.

The same sasjs cbd deploys to any of them - the target in your config decides which.

docs.title: Built on it
docs.text:
Data Controller for SAS - a governed, audited interface for business users to load and edit data in SAS tables - is built entirely on this framework: SAS services compiled and deployed by the CLI, a browser front end on the adapter, and the macro library underneath.

The framework itself is MIT licensed and developed in the open: github.com/sasjs.

docs.title: Three commands
docs.text:
sasjs create myapp -t minimal   # a project with a service, a macro and tests
cd myapp && npm install
sasjs cbd -t mytarget           # compile, build, deploy

cbd is compile, build and deploy in one - and sasjs test runs the project's tests before you get that far.

docs.title: About
docs.text: SASjs is built and maintained by the team behind 4GL Apps and Data Controller for SAS. It started as the internal delivery tooling for our own SAS applications and is published because the same gap exists on almost every SAS estate.

docs.title: Licence
docs.text: Everything in the framework - the CLI, the adapter, the macro library, the lint rules, the server and the VS Code extension - is MIT licensed. You can use it commercially, modify it, and ship it inside your own products, with no runtime fee and no per-seat cost.

docs.title: Getting help
docs.text:
• A bug, or a question about behaviour - open an issue on the repository that owns the component. A reproducible case (the config, the command, the log) gets an answer much faster.
  • A question about how to structure a project - the knowledge base, the CLI documentation and the glossary cover most of it; the chat room covers the rest.
  • Commercial support, training or development - 4GL Apps provides it, including fixed-price delivery of SAS apps built on the framework.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
The framework is developed in the open and contributions are welcome: bug reports, documentation fixes, new lint rules, and pull requests against any component. Each repository has its own contributing notes and commit conventions; the CLI, Core, Adapter and Server all run their own test suites in CI, so a pull request that adds a test is the easiest one to merge.

If you are unsure where a change belongs, open an issue first - the framework spans six repositories and it is not always obvious.

docs.title: Angular
docs.text:
The Angular seed app is the same application as the React one, in Angular: ng new under the hood, the SASjs Adapter configured, a login screen, and a SAS backend in the same repository.

sasjs create my-app -t angular
cd my-app && npm install

Source: sasjs/angular-seed-app.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
my-app/
├── sasjs/                 <- the backend, exactly as in the React seed
│   ├── sasjsconfig.json
│   ├── services/common/
│   └── macros/
├── src/app/
│   ├── sasjs/             <- the adapter instance and its Angular service
│   └── components/        <- including the SAS login form
└── angular.json

The adapter is wrapped in an injectable service, so a component asks for data rather than for SAS:

this.sasjs.request('common/getdata', { areas }).then((res) => {
  this.springs = res.springs
})

docs.title: Develop
docs.text:
npm start               # ng serve, on localhost:4200
sasjs cbd -t myTarget   # compile, build and deploy the services it calls

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
sasjs cbd -t myTarget      # the services
sasjs web -t myTarget      # the front end, packaged as a streaming app
sasjs deploy -t myTarget   # both, into the target

Two Angular-specific notes:

  • remove <base href="/"> from src/index.html if the app is deployed under a subfolder of the SAS server, or the router will resolve against the domain root;
  • ng build --prod writes to dist/, which is what streamConfig.webSourcePath should point at.

docs.title: Backend SAS
docs.text: A SASjs project keeps its SAS code in a folder structure the CLI understands, names its environments as targets, and gets to them with a compile/build/deploy cycle. This page is the shape of all that; Services covers writing the code itself.

docs.title: SAS 9 and Viya are the same project
docs.text:
The delivery mechanism differs; the project does not. A service is a compiled program either way, and the differences are confined to what a target does with it.

SAS 9 Viya What a service becomes a Stored Process in a metadata folder a job definition in a folder, held in Viya's database and managed through its APIs What runs it the Stored Process server (or the workspace server) the compute server, in a compute context you choose Identity client or system identity client or system identity (3.5 and later) Metadata the metadata server PostgreSQL Deployment API the SASjs web service, in metadata the Viya REST APIs Output _webout fileref _webout fileref

Both accept _debug, and both stream arbitrary content to _webout, which is what makes the same adapter work against either.

docs.title: The project
docs.text:
my-project/
├── sasjs/
│   ├── sasjsconfig.json     <- folders and targets
│   ├── services/            <- the services, in subfolders
│   │   ├── common/          <- appinit comes first, on app start
│   │   └── admin/
│   ├── macros/              <- macros, folded into the services that use them
│   ├── programs/            <- SAS programs included by services
│   ├── db/                  <- one folder per library: DDL and load programs
│   ├── tests/               <- one test per service folder
│   └── targets/             <- per-target macros, services and programs
│       ├── sas9/
│       └── viya/
└── src/                     <- the front end, if there is one

sasjs create writes this for you:

npm i -g @sasjs/cli
sasjs create my-project -t sasonly   # backend only
sasjs create my-app -t react         # React front end + this backend

The templates are react, angular, minimal, sasonly and jobs; with no -t you get the plain folder structure. If the folder already holds SAS code, sasjs init adds the tooling without writing over it.

docs.title: The config file
docs.text:
sasjs/sasjsconfig.json declares where the code is and where it goes. The two parts that matter here:

{
  "macroFolders": ["sasjs/macros"],
  "serviceConfig": {
    "serviceFolders": ["sasjs/services/common", "sasjs/services/admin"],
    "initProgram": "sasjs/services/serviceinit.sas"
  },
  "defaultTarget": "viya",
  "targets": [
    {
      "name": "viya",
      "serverType": "SASVIYA",
      "serverUrl": "https://sas.example.com",
      "appLoc": "/Public/app/my-project",
      "contextName": "SAS Job Execution compute context"
    },
    {
      "name": "sas9",
      "serverType": "SAS9",
      "serverUrl": "https://sas9.example.com",
      "appLoc": "/Products/my-project"
    }
  ]
}

appLoc is the folder everything is deployed under - a metadata folder path on SAS 9, a folder path in Viya's content tree (SAS Drive) on Viya. A target can override any root setting, which is how one project deploys different code to different environments.

The full set of keys is documented at sasjsconfig, and the JSON schema is at cli.sasjs.io/sasjsconfig-schema.json - point your editor at it and the file autocompletes.

docs.title: Targets and credentials
docs.text:
sasjs add prompts for a target and writes it to the project config, or to ~/.sasjsrc if you choose the global scope:

sasjs add                  # a new target, prompts for the connection details
sasjs add cred -t myTarget # credentials for an existing target
sasjs auth -t myTarget     # log in / refresh the access token

On Viya that means a client id and secret (SASjs Server keeps the token for you); on SAS 9 it means the user and password used to reach the SASjs web service. sasjs add cred stores them outside the repository, so a target can be committed and its credentials cannot.

docs.title: Compile, build, deploy
docs.text:
sasjs compile          # one program per service, macros embedded
sasjs build            # the deployable artefact for the target
sasjs deploy -t myTarget

or, in one go:

sasjs cbd -t myTarget

Each step is separate because each is useful on its own: compile is what you run to check the SAS is valid to build, build produces something you can inspect and archive, and deploy can be re-run against a new environment without rebuilding. sasjs cb stops before the deploy, and sasjs deploy after a sasjs auth fixes an expired token without recompiling.

docs.title: Jobs, services and tests
docs.text:
• Services answer a caller, so they are compiled with %webout() and deployed under /services/.
  • Jobs answer nobody - they are the batch programs a scheduler runs - so they are compiled without %webout() and deployed under /jobs/.
  • Tests are compiled like services so their results can be returned, and deployed under /tests/.

docs.title: Two things to get right
docs.text:
Code injection. A URL parameter is SAS code as far as the macro processor is concerned. Viya quotes them automatically and SAS 9 does not, so treat a parameter as untrusted input: validate it, or avoid it and send a table instead. sasjs compile quotes what it can, and the macro library has %mf_abort and the %mf_* validation macros for the rest.

Data storage. A SAS data set is a good place for read-only data and a bad place for concurrent writes - there is no row-level locking. If the application writes, write to a database (or SASjs Server's drive, which is a filesystem, not a data layer) rather than to a .sas7bdat that several sessions have open.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Building services on SAS 9 is very straightforward. The below approach will work from 9.3 and upwards.

* compile macros ;
filename mc url "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sasjs/core/main/all.sas";
%inc mc;
* if the above fails, download and compile manually;

* parmcards lets us write to a text file from open code ;
filename ft15f001 temp;
parmcards4;
    * do some sas, any inputs are now already WORK tables;
    data example1 example2;
      set sashelp.class;
    run;
    * send data back;
    %webout(OPEN)
    %webout(ARR,example1) * Array format, fast, suitable for large tables ;
    %webout(OBJ,example2) * Object format, easier to work with ;
    %webout(CLOSE)
;;;;
%mm_createwebservice(path=/User Folders/&sysuserid/My Folder
  , name=testJob
  , code=ft15f001
  , replace=yes)

docs.title: A Viya job without the CLI
Services
docs.text:
There are three main ways to create Services (jobs) in Viya:

  1. Manually through the /SASJobExecution interface
  2. As part of a build process using sasjs-cli
  3. Using code in SAS Studio.

docs.title: SAS Studio
docs.text:
To follow the below, you'll need to compile the MacroCore library into your session. To do this, simply run the following 

filename mc url "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sasjs/core/main/all.sas";
%inc mc;

If you are unable to run the above code, you may not have internet access on your server. In this case, simply click this link and copy paste the content into your SAS session, and run it.

We will create our service using the %mv_createwebservice() macro, which expects SAS code to be passed in as filerefs. This will create the service and provide the necessary precode to retrieve any data that has been sent - and automatically create that data as tables in WORK.

To speed up this demo we are going to use a little known fileref with the alias ft15f001 - when combined with parmcards this allows us to write file content directly in open code, in a similar fashion to datalines and table data.

  filename ft15f001 temp;
  parmcards4;
    * do some sas. All inputs are ALREADY tables in WORK;
    data example1 example2;
      set sashelp.class;
    run;
    * send data back;
    %webout(OPEN)
    %webout(ARR,example1) * Array format, fast, good for large tables;
    %webout(OBJ,example2) * Object format, easier to work with in JS;
    %webout(CLOSE)
  ;;;;
  %mv_createwebservice(path=/Public/myapp/common/appInit,name=testJob,code=ft15f001)

You should now see a URL in the log with a link to your service.

Tip

You can modify your Job Execution service by navigating to YOURVIYASERVER/SASJobExecution and finding it in the folder tree.

docs.title: Built on SASjs: Data Controller
docs.text:
Data Controller for SAS is the framework's proof: a commercial application, in daily use on SAS estates, built with every part of SASjs and deployed by the CLI to whichever platform the customer has.

It exists because editing data in a SAS table is a governance problem, not a technical one. The business needs to correct a value, add a row, approve a change - and the SAS team needs the audit trail, the validation and the approval workflow to be the same in every environment. Data Controller is that interface: an Angular application in the browser, 230 SAS services behind it, and a table-level policy of who may change what.

docs.title: The shape of it
docs.text:
Taken from the project's own configuration:

Services 230 .sas files in seven folders - admin, approvers, auditors, editors, hooks, public, validations Macros 55, in sasjs/macros Front end Angular, on @sasjs/adapter - the same library the seed apps use Targets 13 in one sasjsconfig.json: SAS 9, five Viya environments, seven SASjs Server Deployment sasjs cbd -t <target> - compile, build, deploy, per environment

Thirteen targets is the point. A SAS 9 customer, a Viya customer and the CI server running tests all get the same code from the same repository, compiled the same way, with the differences confined to the target: appLoc, the server type, the context, the credentials.

docs.title: What it demonstrates
docs.text:
• The compile step does the heavy lifting. A deployment carries its services and the macros they use, so a customer upgrade does not mean "also deploy the macro library, in the right order, to the right folders".
  • One adapter, three platforms. The Angular client calls sasjs.request() and does not know whether the answer came from a stored process, a Viya job or SASjs Server.
  • Permissions are the platform's. The folder structure - editors, approvers, auditors - maps onto SAS 9 metadata permissions and Viya folder permissions, so the application's authority model is the estate's, not a second one invented in JavaScript.
  • The framework is usable at application scale. 230 services and 55 macros is not a demo; it is what an application with a real permission model, an audit trail and a validation framework looks like.

docs.title: Where the same patterns are documented
docs.text:
Everything Data Controller relies on is in this site's guides - nothing in it is a private extension of the framework:

  • Services - the unit of backend work, and how it is compiled and deployed.
  • Security - identities, permissions and the trust boundaries the application inherits.
  • Testing - the harness the services are tested with.
  • Deploying to Viya and SAS 9 - what a target does on each.

docs.title: Licensing and availability
docs.text: Data Controller is a commercial product with a free non-commercial licence; SASjs itself, which it is built on, is MIT licensed. See datacontroller.io for the product, and Support for what the team behind both offers commercially.

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
Cross Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) - also referred to as the Same Origin Policy - is a security setting enabled in all modern browsers that prevents a javascript loaded from Server A interfacing with Server B. This exists to prevent a script from, say, www.somedodgysite.com, interfering with a www.myimportantbank.com session.

You'll know you are affected if you see a message such as the following in your browser console:

XMLHttpRequest cannot load http://SASMIDTIER:8080/SASStoredProcess/do.
No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource.
Origin 'http://localhost:54048' is therefore not allowed access.

As this is a browser setting, for development purposes the issue can be side-stepped by launching your browser with the setting disabled. Sample commands for this are listed below:

OS Browser Launch Command Mac Google Chrome open -n -a Google\ Chrome --args --disable-web-security --user-data-dir=/tmp/chrome Mac Brave open -n -a /Applications/Brave\ Browser.app/Contents/MacOS/Brave\ Browser -n --args --incognito --disable-web-security --user-data-dir="/tmp/brave" Linux Chromium chromium --disable-web-security --user-data-dir="/tmp/chrome" Linux Google Chrome google-chrome --disable-web-security --user-data-dir="/tmp/chrome" Windows Google Chrome "C:\Program Files (x86)\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe" --disable-web-security --disable-gpu --user-data-dir=C:\Temp

It does not seem to be possible to enable CORS in modern Firefox browsers.

You will know if you are successful if you see a You are using an unsupported command-line flag: --disable-web-security. Stability and security will suffer. message.

Note - even with CORS enabled you still may be unable to connect to SAS (9 or Viya) if whitelisting is enabled. Also, if you are pushing your web app to a server outside of SAS, you will still have the CORS issue.

To resolve this you will need to ask your administrator, and perhaps offer them the guidance below.

docs.title: SAS 9 EBI
docs.text:
To fix the issue on SAS EBI, open SAS Management Console and navigate through Application Management -> Configuration Manager -> SAS Application Infrastructure.

Right click / properties and add your target url to the following property: sas.web.csrf.referers.knownHosts

Some points to note about this list of urls:

  • They are comma separated
  • The domain should include the trailing slash/
  • The domain can include a partial path for further security, eg https://mydomain.com/usethispart/
  • After modifying the property, the SAS Web Application Server must be restarted.

For more information, see the SAS Middle Tier Admin Guide.

docs.text: A comprehensive article on CORS and CSRF management on SAS Viya is available here.

docs.title: Deploying to SAS 9
docs.text: On SAS 9 a service becomes a Stored Process in a metadata folder, and the compiled program is what the Stored Process server (or the workspace server) executes. Deployment is the act of creating those Stored Processes and their folder tree.

docs.title: One-off: the web service in metadata
docs.text:
sasjs deploy does not write to metadata directly. It runs the generated deployment script through a Stored Process web service in metadata - the SASjs web service - and that program creates the folders and Stored Processes.

That web service is a one-off setup per metadata server, done by an administrator, and the CLI expects it at a fixed location. If a deployment fails at the point of execution with a 404 from /SASStoredProcess/, the web service is what is missing.

Without it there is still a route: sasjs build writes the SAS deployment script as part of the build output, and that script can be run by hand in SAS Studio or Enterprise Guide. It creates the same Stored Processes, under your own identity rather than the web server's - which matters if the services need to write where only the service account can.

docs.title: The target
docs.text:
{
  "name": "sas9",
  "serverType": "SAS9",
  "serverUrl": "https://sas9.example.com",
  "appLoc": "/Products/my-project"
}
Setting Meaning serverUrl the web tier - the same host that answers /SASStoredProcess/ appLoc the metadata folder the project deploys into; created if it does not exist serverType SAS9

Credentials are the user and password that reach that web service, added with sasjs add cred -t sas9 and kept outside the repository.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
sasjs cbd -t sas9

or the steps separately:

sasjs compile
sasjs build -t sas9
sasjs deploy -t sas9

What lands under appLoc:

Artefact Where services /services/<folder>/<name> as Stored Processes tests /tests/..., compiled like services so results can be returned jobs /jobs/..., without the %webout() pre-code the front end, with streamConfig.streamWeb /services/<streamServiceName>, a streaming Stored Process

Deploy is idempotent: it overwrites what exists by default, so the same command is a create or an update.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
The fastest check is the CLI's own: run a service and read its log.

sasjs run sasjs/services/common/appinit.sas -t sas9
sasjs job execute /Products/my-project/jobs/nightly -t sas9

A deployed service is also callable in a browser:

https://sas9.example.com/SASStoredProcess/do?_program=/Products/my-project/services/common/getdata

&_debug=131 returns the log with the output. For a pipeline, sasjs job execute and sasjs run leave their logs in sasjsresults, and sasjs logcheck reads them and fails on what SAS printed - which is the difference between "deployed" and "deployed and works".

docs.title: Things that bite on SAS 9
docs.text:
• Permissions are on the folder. Grant access to /Products/my-project and the subfolders decide who can call which service; the deploy runs as you, so a folder the web server cannot read is a service nobody can call.
  • The load balancer. The SAS Load Balancer ships with three parallel multibridge connections, which is low for an application with concurrent users; 5-10 per CPU core is a sensible floor.
  • Encoding. Stored Processes and the metadata server must agree on encoding, or non-ASCII data is mangled in the response. UTF-8 throughout the estate is the only version of this that stays fixed.
  • The web server's identity. Services run under the workspace server's account by default, not yours. A program that needs your LIBNAMEs needs them defined for that account.

  • Frontend deployment - serving the app that calls these services.
  • CORS - when the app is served from somewhere other than SAS.

docs.title: Deploying to Viya
docs.text: On Viya a service becomes a job definition in a folder, and the compute server runs it in a compute context. The folders and jobs are objects in Viya's database, addressed by path and managed through the Viya APIs - there is no directory on the operating system that holds them, so nothing is deployed by copying a file.

docs.title: The target
docs.text:
{
  "name": "viya",
  "serverType": "SASVIYA",
  "serverUrl": "https://sas.example.com",
  "appLoc": "/Public/app/my-project",
  "contextName": "SAS Job Execution compute context"
}
Setting Meaning serverUrl the Viya environment - the host that answers /SASLogon/ and the compute APIs appLoc the folder in Viya's content tree (SAS Drive) the project deploys into; created if it does not exist contextName the compute context the jobs run in - SAS Job Execution compute context when you want the job execution service to run them serverType SASVIYA

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Viya has no password login for automation; the CLI needs a client id and secret, or an access token.

sasjs add                # prompts for serverUrl, client, secret, appLoc, contextName
sasjs auth -t viya       # log in, and hold the token for the following commands

sasjs add writes the client and secret where they are not committed - the project config keeps the target, the credentials stay in the user profile. On an estate with a self-signed certificate, sasjs add --insecure accepts it for that command only; the permanent fix belongs in the target's httpsAgentOptions, or in the certificate chain.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
sasjs cbd -t viya

or the steps separately: sasjs compile, sasjs build -t viya, sasjs deploy -t viya.

What lands under appLoc:

Artefact Where services /services/<folder>/<name> as jobs tests /tests/... jobs /jobs/..., without the %webout() pre-code the front end, with streamConfig.streamWeb /services/<streamServiceName> as a streaming job, plus assets and the logo

Deployment is idempotent - it overwrites - so the same command creates or updates.

docs.title: Streaming the front end
docs.text:
With streamConfig.streamWeb set, sasjs build packages the built front end (from webSourcePath, build/ or dist/ depending on your framework) into services that the adapter can request, and the whole application is served by Viya: no web server to host, no CORS to configure, and the same folder permissions that protect the data protect the app.

"streamConfig": {
  "streamWeb": true,
  "streamWebFolder": "web",
  "webSourcePath": "build",
  "streamServiceName": "My App",
  "streamLogo": "logo.png"
}

The CLI prints the app's URL after a deploy with streaming enabled.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
sasjs run sasjs/services/common/appinit.sas -t viya    # run a program in a compute session
sasjs job execute /Public/app/my-project/jobs/nightly -t viya

A deployed service is callable through the job execution service:

https://sas.example.com/SASJobExecution?_PROGRAM=/Public/app/my-project/services/common/getdata&_debug=131

Both run and job execute leave a log in sasjsresults, and sasjs logcheck reads those logs and fails on errors - which is what catches the run that reports success and printed ERROR 22-322 anyway.

docs.title: Things that bite on Viya
docs.text:
• The context decides the identity. runServerAs and reuseServerProcesses on the compute context are how a service account is used and how SAS processes are reused between requests. Without reuseServerProcesses, every request pays the session start.
  • streamWebFolder is a folder in the content tree, not an OS directory: the front end's files are objects in Viya, and that folder's permissions are what decide who can fetch the app.
  • Encoding and locale come from the compute session, not from the adapter. A context with a different encoding from your development sessions will change what your proc sql compares.
  • The token expires. sasjs deploy fails on an expired token with a 401 or 403; sasjs auth -t viya re-authenticates, and sasjs deploy alone finishes the job without recompiling.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• SAS 9 - the same project, deployed to metadata.
  • Frontend deployment - the options for serving the app that calls these services.
  • Viya notes - compute context, server reuse and the REST APIs.

docs.title: Design
docs.text: Save yourself a lot of rework by getting at least a rough idea of what you want to build, before you build it!

docs.title: User Experience
docs.text: The frontend design process is split between UX (User Experience, the overall flow) and UI (the User Interface, the actual look and feel). An example of a User Experience might be "A user can access any feature on the site in 4 clicks or less".

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Here is a list of useful tools for quickly mocking up a potential user experience

  • lucidchart.com - great for diagrams
  • mockplus
  • balsamiq - wireframes

docs.title: User Interface
docs.text:
You save a lot of rework when building frontend apps if you can clearly specify what the app should look like before you build it. One way to build apps quickly is to follow consistent style frameworks. If you're looking to build something more bespoke, then it really makes sense to leverage a design tool.

SAS provide some great guidance for building visually appealing interfaces - see: https://communities.sas.com/html/assets/breports/index.html. More from the SAS design team here: https://medium.com/sas-software-design.

docs.title: Figma
docs.text:
Figma is a web based tool (although there are desktop versions) which means you can access your work from any machine. It comes highly recommended from us for a number of reasons:

  • Free to use
  • Send links to your designs
  • A developer can extract each object (eg as vectors), and exact CSS attributes
  • Design screens that respond to screen size changes

It's a professional tool, and well worth spending an hour or so to learn about.

Link: https://www.figma.com

docs.title: Sketch
docs.text: Sketch - a great desktop tool, used primarily on macs. Very powerful for drawing images and standalone graphics.

docs.title: HTML Character Codes
docs.text:
You can spice (🌶) up your page(📃) with a special character codes (🌈) to make it more fun and readable! You can do this by entering the UTF-8 characters directly in your code - however this can occasionally cause problems when copy pasting into different editors (eg WLATIN1, or SAS Enterprise Guide in some windows instances).

An alternative is to use HTML escape codes. So for instance, use 🖨 to represent 🖨.

A useful website for finding / searching for such codes is here: https://html-css-js.com/html/character-codes/icons/.

docs.title: Icons
docs.text:
An alternative to special characters is to use dedicated icon sets. This provides a broader range of images, without necessarily involving the load of an image (they are often embedded within CSS in Base64 or SVG format, or contain large numbers of images in a single PNG)

The great thing is that they can be easily added to your page with a simple tag.

Examples of icon sets:

  • Streamline: https://streamlineicons.com
  • Clarity: https://clarity.design/icons
  • Linea: https://linea.io/

docs.title: Frameworks
docs.text:
It's possible to build good looking apps quickly without having to specify every detail if you can follow existing style guides / frameworks. Choices include:

  • Semantic ui - with a specific version for React
  • Clarity Design - Angular but will soon support React / Vue also
  • Material Design - built by Google
  • Fluent UI - built by Microsoft

docs.title: Image Editing
docs.text:
• https://svgtopng.com
  • https://www.photopea.com - adobe like
  • https://onlinepngtools.com/convert-png-to-jpg - for adding background in png
  • https://www.calculatorsoup.com/calculators/math/ratios.php - maintaining ratio stuff

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: It's said that quality of software is measured by the quality of it's documentation!

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
As a minimum, the following guides should be produced for each app:

  • User Guide
  • Configuration Guide
  • Deployment Guide
  • Developer Guide

docs.title: Building Documentation
docs.text:
Whilst the concept of "word documents on sharepoint sites" is still etched into the skulls of many, there are alternatives available if your firewalls allow. Whilst proprietary office formats and rich text editors are user friendly, they don't fit easily and transparently into source control and continuous integration workflows.

The primary Text Based markup options are MarkDown (md) and reStructuredText (rst). Markdown is easier to learn, whilst RST format is more flexible (can generate PDFs and also provide documentation within code files).

docs.title: README
docs.text:
Suitable for small projects, all four guides could be added to a single README file in the root of your repo. Using a tool such as markdown-to-html you can even convert your README into a nicely formatted HTML page as part of your build process.

    markdown "$MYPROJECT/README.md" > "$BUILDLOC/deploy/README.html"

docs.title: Docsify
docs.text:
We love this tool so much it is now our primary documentation mechanism, and you will find it in all our seed apps. The template documentation site is also on github pages and you can see it here: https://sasjs.github.io/docs

The docsify project documentation is here: https://docsify.js.org/#/

docs.title: MkDocs
docs.text: This is a great tool for generating a static HTML site where each page can be easily written using MarkDown. This page you are reading was built with MkDocs, as well as the documentation site for Data Controller.

docs.title: SAS Markdown
docs.text:
If you want your code in SAS format inside MkDocs markdown, make sure you are using the most recent version (1+) and add the following to your mkdocs.yml file:

theme:
  name: canBeAnything-UseExistingOneIfThere
  highlightjs: true
  hljs_languages:
      - SAS

Then when you are writing code, just put sas on the first line of the code block, eg: 

  ```sas
  data some sas;
    set formatted nicely;
  run;
  ```
You can display in any one of 189 different languages this way.

Contributions Welcome

With an MkDoks site like this, you can click on any section in the mkdocs site and make edits directly in github. If you find any broken links or typos, or would like to add more sections this site - go right ahead! Your change will be submitted as a PR.

Doc Tip

You can even make tips like this! Read on

To create a "tip" like you see above, or the "note" above it, you first need to enable the extension in your mkdocs.yml like so:

markdown_extensions:
  - admonition

Then you can write syntax like follows:

!!! note "note title"
   This is a note
!!! warning "warning title"
   This is a warning
!!! error "error title"
   This is an error
!!! tip "tip title"
   This is a tip

For more info, see docs.

docs.title: DoxyGen
docs.text:
DoxyGen is a commandline tool that can generate a number of output formats, similar to Sphinx. More suitable for documenting code, than generating standalone docs (although it can do that also).

The Macro Core library is documented this way. The following is an example from the mv_webout() macro:

 /**
   @file mv_webout.sas
   @brief Send data to/from the SAS Viya Job Execution Service
   @details This macro should be added to the start of each Job Execution
   Service, **immediately** followed by a call to:

         %mv_webout(FETCH)

     This will read all the input data and create same-named SAS datasets in the
     WORK library.  You can then insert your code, and send data back using the
     following syntax:

         data some datasets; * make some data ;
         retain some columns;
         run;

         %mv_webout(OPEN)
         %mv_webout(ARR,some)  * Array format, fast, suitable for large tables ;
         %mv_webout(OBJ,datasets) * Object format, easier to work with ;
         %mv_webout(CLOSE)


   @param action Either OPEN, ARR, OBJ or CLOSE
   @param ds The dataset to send back to the frontend
   @param _webout= fileref for returning the json
   @param fref= temp fref
   @param dslabel= value to use instead of the real name for sending to JSON
   @param fmt= change to N to strip formats from output

   <h4> Dependencies </h4>
   @li mp_jsonout.sas
   @li mf_getuser.sas

   @version Viya 3.3
   @author Allan Bowe

 **/

Notice the following:

  • file - filename
  • brief - a title for the file
  • details - a long description, HTML can be embedded. Indent by 4 spaces to format content as code.
  • param - a description of each parameter. Keyword parameters have an = suffix.
  • dependencies - not part of the doxygen spec but used by the sasjs-cli to compile macro calls so that each service contains all relevant macros (and no extra macros)
  • version - used in the macrocore library to denote the earliest known version in which the code will run
/**
  @details this is my detailed explanation.
  This part is indented 2 spaces.

      %* this is a SAS comment, note the style - avoids the header being closed;
      %* it is indented 6 spaces (4 spaces from previous non code line);
**/

docs.title: Sphinx
docs.text:
Primarily used for writing in rst format, sphinx is a very powerful documentation builder, built in python and used for all the official python documentation. The founder of this language went on to launch readthedocs.org a hosting platform for Sphinx-built sites.

Some useful resources:

  • Getting started video
  • Online RST renderer: https://rst.ninjs.org
  • RST Table generator
  • Cheatsheet: https://thomas-cokelaer.info/tutorials/sphinx/rest_syntax.html

docs.title: TypeDoc
docs.text:
The good thing about using typescript to build your frontend is that it can auto-generate a lot of documentation as types etc can be inferred from the syntax. The SASjs library is documented this way - adapter.sasjs.io.

More info available here.

docs.title: Do you have examples of SAS apps built with the SASjs framework?
docs.text: We have a list of public SAS apps in github repositories available here - using these you can see examples of the configuration used to build SASjs apps. There is also a commercial app built with the framework that has been deployed to customers in several countries - it's called Data Controller for SAS

docs.title: What are the Minimum Requirements for building Apps on SAS?
docs.text:
To build apps on SAS you need SAS Viya 3.4 and above, or SAS 9.3 and above with Stored Process Server.

You cannot create web apps on SAS with University Edition.

To check if you have SAS Viya, open SAS Studio, click your user profile and click "About".

If you are using Enterprise Guide, then simply run:

data _null_;
  length url $128;
  rc=METADATA_GETURI("Stored Process Web App",url);
  putlog 'Your SAS 9 url is: ' url;
run;

docs.title: Which Browsers Does SASjs Support?
docs.text:
With the right polyfills your SASjs app can support a very wide range of browsers, however the question is - do you really want to? There can be a lot of edge cases to cover and support.

For guidance you might consider following SAS Institute's browser support policy. Note the diminishing support for IE.

docs.title: I want to help, but I’m not a developer. Are there any ways for non-coders to contribute?
docs.text:
1. Answer questions from new users in the community channels
  2. Write instruction manuals or commit to the docs
  3. Make tutorial videos

docs.title: Frontend Deployment
docs.text:
Deployment is the process of taking the app you have built, and putting it somewhere that others can access it! There are many ways to deploy a SAS web app - we will describe the following:

  • SAS Web Server
  • Third party Server
  • Streaming Apps
  • Desktop Apps

Another option, not described here, is to deploy your frontend as content on a webdav server.

docs.title: SAS Web Server
docs.text: For Single Page Web Apps you are highly recommended to upload them to the static content area of the SAS web server. This avoids the need to configure serverUrl and for administrators to whitelist any additional servers.

docs.title: SAS9 Deploy
docs.text:
The standard location of the static content area on the SAS9 web server is !SASCONFIG/LevX/Web/WebServer/htdocs. For larger customers, your web server may be on a different server to the application server. The app should go into a subfolder (eg htdocs/YOURAPP). It will then be visible ad YOURSERVER.COM/YOURAPP.

To find the server name, you can run the following code:

data _null_;
  length url $128;
  rc=METADATA_GETURI("Stored Process Web App",url);
  putlog 'Your SAS 9 url is: ' url;
run;

docs.title: Viya Deploy
docs.text:
The standard location of the static content area on the Viya web server is /var/www/html.

If this isn't right you can take the following advice courtesy of Kurt Bremser in this communities thread:

Check if httpd uses a special config file (display the command line with ps -f).

If not, simply search for httpd.conf. Within that, you find the location of DocumentRoot.

docs.title: Third Party Server
docs.text:
With this approach you have a lot of possibilities, as you can use any technology you like for the backend, including a database, and just use SAS when analytics are needed.

This approach typically requires administrator support, as your domain will need to be whitelisted from SAS.

docs.title: Streaming Apps
docs.text:
Streaming apps are served directly from the SAS logical folder tree - ie Metadata in SAS 9 or SAS Drive in Viya.

The benefits are:

  • No need for a web server
  • No client/secret needed
  • Nothing to whitelist
  • Can be done by ANY SAS user (as last resort, can deploy to home directory)
  • Ability to secure the frontend using folder permissions (not available to other methods)

The downsides:

  • Performance. The app will be much less responsive (ie, slower) than if you deploy to the web server. This is due to the cost of the first request, however the second / subsequent requests are typically cached by the browser so are much faster.
  • Efficiency. Linked to the above, storage and throughput wise it's not an efficient way to deploy nor serve a web app.
  • Limited functionality. The vast majority of apps will work fine, but there are some edge cases that are not yet handled.

docs.title: Streaming App Configuration
docs.text:
Another great thing about streaming apps is that they require no changes to your frontend! It's simply some additional config in the compilation process, specifically the streamConfig attribute.

This can go either at root or target level in your sasjsconfig.json file. The relevant attributes are:

  • streamWeb - set to true to create the streaming app as part of the sasjs compile process.
  • webSourcePath - the local folder containing the built version of the app. If you are writing vanilla js, it's just the folder containing your index.html. For React/Angular, it could be your dist or build folder.
  • streamServiceName - the name of the service containing the index.html. This is a SAS service named clickme by default.
  • streamWebFolder - the name of the SAS logical folder under which all the web content will be stored.

docs.title: Streaming App Compilation
docs.text:
When running sasjs web (also executed as part of sasjs compile), the SASjs CLI will open up the index.html in the webSourcePath folder and migrate a copy of every dependency (JS, CSS, images, sounds, etc) into the sasjsbuild/services/$(streamWebFolder) folder.

For SAS 9, all content will be converted into Stored Processes. This is achieved by base64 encoding the content and streaming it back with the appropriate content-type.

For Viya, content is deployed as actual files in SAS Drive. This is a lot more space efficient. In addition, to avoid the issue with Viya-streamed files whereby a redirect occurs to a temporary UUID from the files service, we call the index.html with an extra parameter - _debug=2. This wraps the response in an iframe, and by embedding some extra attributes, we surface the child contents so it looks like the main page, however a user-friendly URL is retained.

To clarify - all you need to do to achieve the above is run sasjs compile.

docs.title: Streaming App Build
docs.text:
The build process takes all the compiled content in the sasjsbuild folder and turns it into a build pack. The build pack comes in two forms:

  • JSON file (used exclusively when autodeploying to SAS Viya using the REST APIs)
  • SAS file (can be used by both SAS 9 or Viya to deploy all content programmatically)

The build pack is created by running sasjs build. The name of the pack is determined by the buildOutputFileName attribute, and takes the target name by default.

docs.title: Streaming App Deployment
docs.text:
One way to deploy a streamed app is to simply run the generated SAS file. If you can host this somewhere, you can deploy a SAS App to any customer with just two lines of code - here's an example. Using this approach, the link to the final app will be shown in the SAS log.

For automated (CI/CD) development, you will probably want to do this using the command line. For that you will need to ensure the deployServicePack attribute is true. With this, you can autodeploy by simply running sasjs deploy. The link to the final app will be shown in the console.

Note - you will first need to have authenticated to your SAS server using sasjs auth.

docs.title: Desktop Apps
docs.text:
Another option for building apps is to actually host them on the desktop. Using technologies such as Electron, or React Native, you can build apps that are saved on the users desktop or mobile device.

This will again require server whitelisting, the use of a CLIENT/SECRET, or a dedicated (Third party) web server.

docs.title: Frontend web
docs.text:
A SASjs front end is an ordinary web application - React, Angular, or plain JavaScript - that talks to SAS services through the adapter. There is no template language in the middle: the browser renders the interface, SAS answers with data.

That separation is the whole design. The front end can be built, tested and reviewed with the tools web developers already use, by people who do not write SAS; the services can be written and tested by people who do not write JavaScript. Both live in one repository, and the CLI deploys both.

docs.title: What not to do
docs.text:
The traditional SAS approach is to generate the interface from SAS: put statements in a DATA step, or proc stream, writing HTML out of _webout. It works for a form. It stops working at the first feature that needs state, routing or a component library - the markup is now a string literal inside a SAS program, with no build step, no syntax checking and nobody willing to change it.

SASjs supports streaming content to _webout - that is how a built application is delivered - but the HTML it streamed was written by a front end developer, not by a DATA step.

docs.title: Three ways to serve the same application
docs.text:
Approach How When Streamed from SAS sasjs web packages the built front end as services; SAS serves the index, the assets and the API one deployment target, no separate web server, no CORS - works on SAS 9 and Viya Static host, adapter to SAS build/ or dist/ goes to any static host or CDN; the adapter calls SAS directly a CDN or existing web tier, and the SAS estate can accept cross-origin requests SASjs Server app portal upload the built app as a zip; the server hosts it, with per-user and per-group permissions SAS 9 shops without a web tier, demos, internal tools

All three run the same application code and the same services. The difference is who serves the files.

docs.title: Streamed from SAS
docs.text:
This is the option most SAS estates end up choosing, because it removes the two things that usually block a SAS web application: a web server nobody wants to own, and a CORS policy nobody wants to change.

"streamConfig": {
  "streamWeb": true,
  "streamWebFolder": "web",
  "webSourcePath": "build",
  "streamServiceName": "My App"
}

sasjs cbd -t myTarget compiles the services, packages the front end into streaming services, and deploys both. The CLI prints the URL. See Deploying to Viya and SAS 9 for what that means on each platform.

docs.title: Developing locally
docs.text:
The front end runs on localhost and calls a real SAS environment, which is the fastest loop there is - the alternative is rebuilding and redeploying to see a CSS change.

npm start               # the dev server
sasjs cbd -t myTarget   # deploy the services it calls

Because the origin differs, the SAS side has to allow it: cors and whitelist settings on Viya, or the equivalent on the web tier. CORS covers the details, including the version that catches everybody out - a browser request that works from curl and fails from the app is a preflight.

docs.title: Choosing a framework
docs.text:
• React and Angular are the two seed applications: real apps, with login, a request history and a SASjs backend already wired up.
  • sasjs create my-app -t minimal is a small application in plain JavaScript, which is the fastest way to see the adapter without a framework.
  • Anything else works too: the adapter is a library, not a framework, and a Vue or Svelte or htmx front end uses it the same way.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Frontend deployment - the deployment options in more detail.
  • State management - where the application's data lives, and what to fetch again.
  • CORS - when the app and SAS are on different origins.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: If you'd like to see a new item added, feel free to raise an issue or PR!

docs.title: appLoc
docs.text:
Relevant to: Adapter, CLI, VSCE

The "appLoc" represents the "app location" in terms of where the backend web services are stored in the logical folder tree (eg SAS Drive on Viya, or metadata in SAS 9).

It does not represent a physical path, such as a linux directory or windows folder. It's more analagous to WebDav (collection of parent/child relationships).

The appLoc will be deployed with the following structure (folders will only be created if relevant artefacts are compiled):

  • $(appLoc)/services/(subfolder)
  • $(appLoc)/jobs/(subfolder)
  • $(appLoc)/tests/macros
  • $(appLoc/tests/jobs
  • $(appLoc/tests/services

docs.title: Adapter Specific guidance
docs.text:
By defining the appLoc in the SASjs config, the sasjs.request() method can use a relative path (without leading slash), meaning that the app can be easily moved (or deployed elsewhere).

If the request() method is used with a leading slash, the appLoc is ignored. If request() is used without a leading slash, the appLoc must be provided in the sasjs config object.

docs.title: Includes
docs.text:
Relevant to: CLI, VSCE

SAS Includes (coming from the programFolders array) can be inserted into any Primary Artefact (Job or Service or Test). They are essentially 'arbitrary code blocks'. More information available here

docs.title: Macros
docs.text:
Relevant to: CLI, VSCE

SAS Macros (coming from the macroFolders array) should be in a file with the same name as the macro itself. Each macro file should contain just one macro. Macros can be compiled into multiple artefacts. More information here.

docs.title: Programs
docs.text: See includes.

docs.title: Job
docs.text:
Relevant to: CLI, VSCE

A "Job" in SASjs (coming from the jobFolders array) relates to a batch program, which has one or more Data Inputs and (ideally) one Data Output. It is one of the three Primary Artefacts. Additional programs and macros may be compiled as precode.

Jobs may take a long time to execute. Lineage can be generated for jobs using the sasjs doc command (so long as the correct headers are set).

docs.title: Service
docs.text:
Relevant to: Adapter, CLI, VSCE

A "Service" in SASjs (coming from the serviceFolders array) relates to an 'on demand' process with zero or more Service Inputs and one or more Service Outputs. Those inputs/outputs can be anything, but are typically JSON. Services should be designed to run as fast as possible, and never longer than 5 minutes (a common timeout threshold)

When services are compiled, additional precode is added to enable the %webout() macro. This macro converts adapter inputs to WORK tables, and allows further WORK tables to be sent back in a specific JSON format. Depending on the serverType, the underlying webout macro is either:

  • mm_webout.sas (used for SAS9 EBI)
  • ms_webout.sas (used for SASjs Server)
  • mv_webout.sas (used for Viya)

docs.title: Target
docs.text:
Relevant to: CLI, VSCE

A Target in SASjs represents a configuration against which the app will be deployed. Example items for a configuration include:

  • serverType (eg SAS9, SASJS, SASVIYA)
  • serverUrl (the url of the server)
  • appLoc (the logical folder to which the SAS web services will be deployed)

docs.title: Test
docs.text:
Relevant to: CLI

Tests can be written for Jobs, Services, or Macros. They are compiled as Services to enable the webout() macro for sending the test results. More information on tests is available here

docs.title: Where is my Server?
docs.text:
If you're on a new site, you don't always know where your SAS Server is!

There are two options to find out programmatically:

docs.title: METADATA_GETURI
docs.text:
Probably the quickest and easiest:

data _null_;
  length url $128.;
  call missing(url);
  rc = METADATA_GETURI("Stored Process Web App",url);
  put url=;
run;

docs.title: mm_getwebappsrvprops
docs.text:
This macro gets a bunch of properties relating to web servers, however it's possible that access may be restricted, depending on the metadata permissions at your site.

%mm_getwebappsrvprops(outds= some_ds)
data _null_;
    set some_ds(where=(name='webappsrv.server.url'));
    put value=;
run;

docs.title: Load Balancing
docs.text: The SAS Load Balancer comes with 3 parallel (multibridge) connections by default. This must be increased! A good minimum is 5-10 per CPU core.

docs.title: Viya platform notes
docs.text:
SAS Viya is the new kid on the block and the future for the SAS platform. It has a blazingly fast in-memory, scalable architecture and is built with developers in mind.

Here are some relevant tips & tricks to help from an app-development perspective.

docs.title: Server Restart
docs.text:
This is necessary after configuring settings such as whitelisting. Log onto the box as an admin and execute the following commands:

sudo /etc/init.d/sas-viya-all-services stop
# open top or htop and kill any redundant / remaining SAS processes
sudo /etc/init.d/sas-viya-all-services start

docs.title: Shared Account and Server re-use
docs.text: Server pooling and the use of a shared OS account are both possible from Viya 3.5 - the documentation is here (and communities articles are available here and here)

docs.title: Compute setup
docs.text:
If running on the SAS box, first source /opt/sas/viya/config/consul.conf to set the SSL_CERT_FILE. Next, navigate to /opt/sas/viya/home/bin.

To create your profile (if you haven't done this already) run ./sas-admin profile init.

Then, ./sas-admin auth login to authenticate (with your own credentials). Next, ./sas-admin compute credentials create and use the credentials you would like the new compute context to use (the equivalent of the SAS 9 sassrv account).

To validate, you should see these creds on the /credentials/domains?start=10 endpoint.

Now run the following command: sudo systemctl restart sas-viya-runlauncher-default

Next up, log onto SASEnvironment Manager (as admin user), Contexts, View Compute Contexts. You can either create a new profile, or modify the existing "SAS Job Execution compute context".

Scroll down and add the following attribute / value pairs:

Status Attribute Value Mandatory runServerAs the user id we used in the ./sas-admin compute credentials create step above Mandatory reuseServerProcesses true Optional serverInactiveTimeout Time in seconds before the server times out. Will otherwise time out when there are no active sessions. Default is 600 (10 mins). We recommend 1800 or longer. Optional allowXCMD true or false Optional unsafeJobCharacters Contains the characters that the compute session should remove from any variable that is provided to a job for execution. By default, the following characters are removed: & (ampersand), ” (double quotation mark), ; (semicolon), ’ (single quotation mark), and % (percent sign). If set to "" the feature is disabled.

With this feature enabled, your end user ID will be SYS_COMPUTE_SESSION_OWNER instead of SYSUSERID.

Note - a server restart is not required.

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
If you are hosting your web app on a web server (like you should) then there is really not much to consider regarding images, other than for you to minimise file sizes to improve app load times. Images are often cached so subsequent loads are less of an issue.

If you are streaming HTML from SAS though, images are more of a challenge. This is where base64 encoding comes in. Essentially this technique lets you save an image as a long string.

There are many online services that will convert an image into a Base64 string for you, eg: https://base64.guru/converter/encode/image.

When streaming through the SAS _webout fileref, be aware that you are likely to hit the line length restriction. To avoid this, set a large value for lrecl or ensure that your data is streamed byte by byte.

If you use the sasjs-cli tool, this part will be handled for you.

docs.title: React
docs.text:
The React seed app is a working application, not a skeleton: create-react-app under the hood, the SASjs Adapter configured, a login screen, a request history, and a SAS backend in the same repository.

sasjs create my-app -t react
cd my-app && npm install

Source: sasjs/react-seed-app.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
my-app/
├── sasjs/                 <- the backend
│   ├── sasjsconfig.json   <- targets for viya, sas9 and a SASjs Server
│   ├── services/common/   <- appinit.sas, getdata.sas
│   ├── services/serviceinit.sas
│   └── macros/
├── src/                   <- the React application
│   ├── App.js
│   ├── api/               <- the adapter instance and the request helpers
│   └── components/        <- including the SAS login form
└── package.json

The adapter is created once, in src/api, from the target that sasjs deploys to:

import { SASjs } from '@sasjs/adapter'

const sasjs = new SASjs({
  serverUrl: process.env.REACT_APP_SERVER_URL,
  appLoc: process.env.REACT_APP_APPLOC,
  serverType: 'SASVIYA'
})

export const getData = (areas) => sasjs.request('common/getdata', { areas })

The same component then works against Viya, SAS 9 and SASjs Server: the adapter hides which one is underneath.

docs.title: Develop
docs.text:
npm start               # the React dev server on localhost:3000
sasjs cbd -t myTarget   # compile, build and deploy the services it calls

While developing, the front end runs locally and calls a remote SAS environment - which means the SAS environment has to allow the request: see CORS and the target's cors/whitelist settings. If you would rather have no server at all in the loop, point the adapter at a SASjs Server on your own machine.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
The front end and the services deploy separately, and the CLI does both:

sasjs cbd -t myTarget      # the services
sasjs web -t myTarget      # the front end, packaged as a streaming app
sasjs deploy -t myTarget   # both, into the target

With streamConfig.streamWeb set, the front end is packaged as services and served from the SAS folder tree - on Viya from SAS Drive, on SAS 9 from metadata - so there is no separate web server to run and no CORS to configure. Without it, deploy build/ to whatever serves your static assets and point the adapter at SAS.

The seed app's sasjsconfig.json has a target for each - viya, sas9 and sasjs - so switching environments is -t viya versus -t sas9.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text: Each component is released independently, from its own repository, with semantic versioning driven by conventional commit messages. There is no single "SASjs version": a project pins the packages it uses, and the CLI reports what it has.

docs.title: Where each one lives
docs.text: Component Package Releases CLI @sasjs/cli sasjs/cli releases Macro Core @sasjs/core sasjs/core releases Adapter @sasjs/adapter sasjs/adapter releases Server @sasjs/server sasjs/server releases - executables as well as the package Lint @sasjs/lint sasjs/lint releases VS Code extension sasjs/vscode-extension releases

docs.title: Checking what you have
docs.text:
sasjs --version                      # the CLI you are running
npm view @sasjs/cli version          # the newest published version
npm outdated                         # what a project is behind on

A project's package.json is the place to pin Core and the adapter. The CLI is usually global, which is why sasjs --version is part of any bug report.

docs.title: How a release happens
docs.text:
Commits carry conventional messages - feat:, fix:, docs:, and a scope where it helps. Merging to the default branch runs the test suite, and a release is cut from the commit messages: a feat: is a minor version, a fix: a patch, a BREAKING CHANGE: a major one. The changelog is generated from the same messages, so the release notes are the commit history rather than a separate document that drifts from it.

That has one consequence worth knowing: the version number tells you the nature of the change, and the release notes tell you the detail. A fix: release can still change behaviour if the previous behaviour was wrong.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
• Core is embedded at compile time, so upgrading it means recompiling and redeploying - which is also why an upgrade cannot break a service you have not rebuilt.
  • The CLI is global; upgrade it with npm i -g @sasjs/cli.
  • The adapter is a project dependency, so a normal npm install brings it in; check the release notes for breaking changes before a major.
  • Server is a single binary: download the release, verify its checksum, and replace it - the settings and the drive live outside the binary.

docs.title: Following along
docs.text:
• Watch the repository you depend on (Releases only) for the releases that matter to you.
  • The SASjs chat room and LinkedIn carry announcements.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
If you have followed the conventional-commit standard you can now generate a version number according to sementic-versioning along with relevant release notes.

There are two great command-line tools for managing a release:

1) standard-version - will generate a CHANGELOG and the version number but won't push the release

2) semantic-release - will manage everything including the release. A great guide is available here
