docs.title: SASjs Adapter
docs.text:
The SASjs adapter is a JS library and a set of SAS Macros that handle the communication between the frontend app and backend SAS services.

There are three parts to consider:

  1. JS request / response
  2. SAS inputs / outputs
  3. Configuration

docs.title: JS Request / Response
docs.text:
To install the library you can simply run npm install @sasjs/adapter or include a <script> tag with a reference to our CDN.

Full technical documentation is available here. The main parts are:

docs.title: Instantiation
docs.text:
The following code will instantiate an instance of the adapter:

let sasJs = new SASjs.default(
  {
    appLoc: "/Your/SAS/Folder",
    serverType:"SAS9"
  }
);
More on the config later.

docs.title: SAS Logon
docs.text:
The login process can be handled directly, as below, or as a callback function to a SAS request.

sasJs.logIn('USERNAME','PASSWORD'
  ).then((response) => {
  if (response.isLoggedIn === true) {
    console.log('do stuff')
  } else {
    console.log('do other stuff')
  }
}

docs.title: Request / Response
docs.text:
A simple request can be sent to SAS in the following fashion:

sasJs.request("/path/to/my/service", dataObject)
  .then((response) => {
    // all tables are in the response object, eg:
    console.log(response.tablewith2cols1row[0].COL1.value)
  })
We supply the path to the SAS service, and a data object. The data object can be null (for services with no input), or can contain one or more tables in the following format:

let dataObject={
    "tablewith2cols1row": [{
        "col1": "val1",
        "col2": 42
    }],
    "tablewith1col2rows": [{
        "col": "row1"
    }, {
        "col": "row2"
    }]
};

There are optional parameters such as a config object and a callback login function.

The response object will contain returned tables and columns. Table names are always lowercase, and column names uppercase.

The adapter will also cache the logs (if debug enabled) and even the work tables. For performance, it is best to keep debug mode off.

docs.title: SAS Inputs / Outputs
docs.text:
The SAS side is handled by a number of macros in the macro core library.

The following snippet shows the process of SAS tables arriving / leaving: 

/* fetch all input tables sent from frontend - they arrive as work tables */
%webout(FETCH)

/* some sas code */
data some sas tables;
  set from js;
run;

%webout(OPEN)  /* open the JSON to be returned */
%webout(OBJ,some) /* `some` table is sent in object format */
%webout(ARR,sas) /* `sas` table is sent in array format, smaller filesize */
%webout(OBJ,tables,fmt=N) /* unformatted (raw) data */
%webout(OBJ,tables,dslabel=newtable) /* rename tables on export */
%webout(OBJ,tables,dslabel=truncated, maxobs=10) /* send back max 10 rows */
%webout(CLOSE) /* close the JSON and send some extra useful variables too */

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Configuration on the client side involves passing an object on startup, which can also be passed with each request. Technical documentation on the SASjsConfig class is available here. The main config items are:

  • appLoc - this is the folder under which the SAS services will be created.
  • serverType - either SAS9 or SASVIYA.
  • serverUrl - the location (including http protocol and port) of the SAS Server. Can be omitted, eg if serving directly from the SAS Web Server, or in streaming mode.
  • debug - if true then SAS Logs and extra debug information is returned.
  • useComputeApi - if true and the serverType is SASVIYA then the REST APIs will be called directly (rather than using the JES web service).
  • contextName - if missing or blank, and useComputeApi is true and serverType is SASVIYA then the JES API will be used.

The adapter supports a number of approaches for interfacing with Viya (serverType is SASVIYA). For maximum performance, be sure to configure your compute context with reuseServerProcesses as true and a system account in runServerAs. This functionality is available since Viya 3.5. This configuration is supported when creating contexts using the CLI.

docs.title: Using JES Web App
docs.text:
In this setup, all requests are routed through the JES web app, at YOURSERVER/SASJobExecution. This is the most reliable method, and also the slowest. One request is made to the JES app, and remaining requests (getting job uri, session spawning, passing parameters, running the program, fetching the log) are made on the SAS server by the JES app.

{
  appLoc:"/Your/Path",
  serverType:"SASVIYA"
}

docs.title: Using the JES API
docs.text:
Here we are running Jobs using the Job Execution Service except this time we are making the requests directly using the REST API instead of through the JES Web App. This is helpful when we need to call web services outside of a browser (eg with the SASjs CLI or other commandline tools). To save one network request, the adapter prefetches the JOB URIs and passes them in the __job parameter.

{
  appLoc:"/Your/Path",
  serverType:"SASVIYA",
  useComputeApi: true
}

docs.title: Using the Compute API
docs.text:
This approach is by far the fastest, as a result of the optimisations we have built into the adapter. With this configuration, in the first sasjs request, we take a URI map of the services in the target folder, and create a session manager - which spawns an extra session. The next time a request is made, the adapter will use the 'hot' session. Sessions are deleted after every use, which actually makes this less resource intensive than a typical JES web app, in which all sessions are kept alive by default for 15 minutes.

{
  appLoc:"/Your/Path",
  serverType:"SASVIYA",
  useComputeApi: true,
  contextName: 'yourComputeContext'
}

docs.title: SASJS-CLI
docs.text:
The CLI tool fulfills a number of purposes:

  • Creation of a project repository in an 'opinionated' way
  • Compilation each service, including all the dependent macros / macro variables and pre / post code
  • Build - creation of the master SAS deployment, including build macros, macro variables, and pre/post code
  • Deployment - tools and utilities for server management and deployment directly from GIT and command line

Full documentation for the CLI is available at https://cli.sasjs.io

docs.title: Demo
docs.text: SASjs was presented to the SAS User Group UK & Ireland in March 2020 as an approach for deploying, executing & scheduling viya jobs. The video is available below.

docs.title: MacroCore Library
docs.text:
The MacroCore library provides routines and helpers for use in SAS side application logic and deployments. It is divided into 5 sections:

  • BASE - Macro functions (mf_*) and macro procedures (mp_*) that can be used in all flavours of SAS. No XCMD is assumed.

  • META - Macros (mm_*) that interface with SAS 9 metadata. No XCMD assumed.

  • METAX - Metadata macros that depend on XCMD, eg those interfacing with the Batch tools.

  • VIYA - Macros that interface with SAS Viya. No XCMD assumed.

Check out the source code and documentation.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
The easest way to make these macros available is to just include them in your session as follows:

filename mc url "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sasjs/core/main/all.sas";
%inc mc;

If you don't have internet access from your SAS session, you can download the macros directly from here and place them in your autoexec, or initialisation file.

A further option might be to git clone the repository, and set up sasautos, eg:

options insert=(sasautos="/your/path/macrocore/base"));
options insert=(sasautos="/your/path/macrocore/meta"));

The final deployment option, if you are building web apps, is Node Package Manager - simply run npm install @sasjs/core in your project repository. Using sasjs-cli you can compile these macros into your web services at build time, and lock them to a particular release.

docs.title: Generating Viya Client & Secret in SAS Studio
docs.text:
The CORE library can be used by an administrator to register a Viya Client & Secret. Execute the following:

filename mc url "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sasjs/core/main/all.sas";
%inc mc;

/* create random client and secret */
%mv_registerclient(outds=clientinfo)

This will generate a URL in the log, which must be followed to generate a refresh code (one time step). Paste that code into the macro below:

/* paste the code below */
%mv_tokenauth(inds=clientinfo,code=xET8ETs74z)
There is now a table in the WORK library containing the access token. The clientinfo table contains the client & secret.

A convenient (but insecure) way to extract these details to the log:

/* extract client, secret & token to the log */
data _null_;
  merge mv_tokenauth clientinfo(drop=error);
  put access_token=;
  put refresh_token=;
  put client_id=;
  put client_secret=;
run;

Warning

Security tokens are like passwords. The above is provided for convenience, but you should avoid writing tokens to log files unless you are very sure of your environment.

docs.title: Calling SAS Viya from SAS 9
docs.text:
When calling SAS Viya from SAS 9, the oauth_bearer=sas_services option is not available. However it is still possible to call the APIs in SAS 9 with proc http in the core library by putting the ACCESS_TOKEN in a macro variable and referring to that variable in the access_token_var= keyword parameter of each viya macro (starting mv_).

Warning

Saving security tokens in project repositories, especially if they are committed to source control, is a security risk - as anyone with access can use them to make modifications on the Viya platform. Be sure to use a secure mechanism such as the %inc from a secure directory, or another approved mechanism for securing these kinds of variables. Avoid writing Access Tokens to log files.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Deploying web apps is generally more secure than, say, Python or R, because the Javascript libraries that are included do not have access to the filesystem. The browser "sandbox" also prevents JS files loaded from a one domain from making calls to another domain (Cross Origin Resource Sharing / CORS). That said, there are still a few security considerations to keep in mind when building apps on SAS.

docs.title: Shared Services account
docs.text:
A shared system account for running web services is preferred as it can enable functionality for users that they cannot (or should not) perform themselves, eg database modifications (and for that, you should seriously consider Data Controlller for SAS®). It can also avoids unix permissions issues, as created files are owned by default under the end user identity.

However - as it is a shared account, the ability to run code under this identity should be appropriately governed. In particular, code injection must be protected against - for this reason, URL parameters are a bad idea, much better to send tables using an adapter such as SASjs.

It is also recommended to ensure you have a secure release process, which includes code review and automated testing, to ensure the safety of your production environment.

docs.title: SAS 9
docs.text:
By default your services will run on a Stored Process server under the shared credentials stored in the SAS General Servers group group (sassrv per factory settings).

It is also possible to run STPs under a Workspace Server context (where end user OS credentials match &sysuserid).

docs.title: SAS Viya
docs.text:
By default, services will run on the SAS Compute server under the client identity. Since Viya 3.5 it is also possible to run under a shared identity, and to pool the session - see documentation.

For enhanced sas viya security you can even determine which users can execute code on a particular context (all authenticated users, or a particular set of users.)

docs.title: SAS Groups
docs.text: As described in this excellent article the recommended approach for creating groups is to follow a convention such as App.<your_app> - and apply this to your SAS App Folder (appLoc) as well as the scope when generating the client (if SAS Viya)

docs.title: Folder Security
docs.text:
The recommended SASjs folder structure is to group services into app subfolders, so that security can be applied at backend. The app itself can also be secured by setting permission on the parent folder. There is one more thing to consider - services can be viewed (and executed) by anyone who has the READ permission, either using the SERVERURL/SASStoredProcess?_action=1063 url or by navigating in SASJobExecution on Viya. Therefore your services should be built in such a way that no damage would be caused if an end user were to accidentally 'click' on one of the services and run it.

This folder structure is enforced when using the sasjs-cli tool.

docs.title: Idempotence
docs.text: Services should be built in such a way that they can be safely executed more than once. This is because it's possible that it WILL be run more than once (eg if the user clicks a button twice in succession).

docs.title: URL Parameters
docs.text:
The use of URL parameters (which are automatically converted to macro variables in a SAS session) should be avoided. Apart from the risk of code injection, there are also a number of reserved variables that may cause unintentional naming conflicts. Use the SASjs adapter instead!

Note that Viya automatically escapes certain characters (eg ;) to reduce this risk.

docs.title: SubResource Integrity
docs.text:
An integrity hash is a checksum of a file - if just one character inside a file is changed, the checksum is totally different. This makes it a great tool for verifying that a CSS or JS file has not been modified since the checksum was generated. Content served over http (without SSL certificates) are extremely susceptible to Man in the Middle (MitM) attacks. For this reason, it is best practice to either bundle all your dependencies inside your app, or apply SubResource Integrity (SRI) checking as per the w3.org spec. The syntax looks like this:

<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/sasjs@1.10.8/index.js"
  integrity="sha256-651B1pxDxaKb9yhXQOUSohZ+Nq9Txfc3gXlX/GSw1RQ="
  crossorigin="anonymous"></script>

If your CSS or JS files are released via github, then they are automatically available with SRI checks using JSDelivr - for instance, to get the latest script tag for SASjs you can just click here and select "SRI".

If your files are elsewhere, or you'd like more control over the build, you can also generate the integrity hash yourself - here is the syntax:

cat myfile.js | openssl dgst -sha384 -binary | openssl enc -base64

docs.title: Third Party Server
docs.text:
By setting up a dedicated web server and whitelisting it within SAS, you can isolate your frontend activities and enable frontend developers to deploy without having to enable access to the SAS Web Server directly.

Web devs can then work locally and push to that server, or work on the server directly. One option for enabling remote (cloud) development is the open-source server edition of vscode: https://github.com/cdr/code-server (note - this won't work with vscodium due to non open-source components.

To whitelist the server in Viya, open Environment Manager -> Configuration -> View -> Definitions and select sas.commons.web.security.cors. Make sure your domain (or *) is entered under allowedHeaders, allowedMethods and AllowedOrigin.

docs.title: target=blank is unsafe
docs.text:
Commonly used to open new tabs, be very careful opening external sites using a naked _target=blank attribute - this opens a vulnerability for hijacking.

To avoid this, simply add a rel="noopener noreferrer" attribute to the anchor tag.

docs.title: Content Security Policy
docs.text:
This is a server setting that restricts the types of content that pages served from your domain can fetch. This might be to specific urls, or types of content (such as inline styles, base64 images, or external JS files). If you are being restricted by CSP policy you will see a message like the one below in your console window:

Content Security Policy: The page's settings blocked the loading of a resource at https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/combine/npm/chart.js@2.9.3,npm/jquery@3.5.1,npm/@sasjs/adapter@1.0.6 ("default-src").

On SAS 9 the CSP configuration can be found in the following file location: !SASCONFIG/Lev1/Web/WebServer/conf/sas.conf

The line to be modified will look something like this: 

Header set Content-Security-Policy "default-src 'self' ; script-src 'unsafe-inline'  https://cdn.jsdelivr.net https://stackpath.bootstrapcdn.com; font-src 'self' data: fonts.gstatic.com;style-src 'self' fonts.googleapis.com"

After modifying the CSP the mid tier will need to be restarted (./sas.servers.mid restart)

Whilst it is often impossible to implement maximally secure settings, the configuration goal should be to enable as few of the 'insecure' ones as possible. More information is available here.

Note that the "default-src" provides a fallback where particular urls (eg font-src) are not specified.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
A service is a SAS program a browser - or another system - can call, and which answers with data. In SASjs it is a .sas file in sasjs/services, compiled by the CLI and deployed to a target, so what runs in production is exactly what was reviewed in the repository.

This page is the end-to-end version: write one, compile it, deploy it, call it.

docs.title: 1. Write the service
docs.text:
A service is ordinary SAS. The only framework-specific part is how it receives input and returns output: %webout().

/**
  @file
  @brief List the springs in an area
  @details Called with the area selected in the app's dropdown.
  <h4> SAS Macros </h4>
  @li mf_abort.sas
**/

/* the table the browser sent arrives as a WORK table, named as it was sent */
%webout(FETCH)

%mf_abort(
  iftrue=(%sysfunc(exist(work.areas))=0),
  msg=No area was supplied
)

proc sql;
  create table springs as
    select * from mydb.springs
    where area in (select area from work.areas);
quit;

%webout(OPEN)
%webout(OBJ,springs)
%webout(CLOSE)

%webout() is supplied by sasjs compile, not by you: the compiler prepends it (and the macros it depends on) to every service and every test, which is why the deployed program has no dependency on SASAUTOS. Its actions are:

Call Does %webout(FETCH) Turns each table the caller sent into a WORK table of the same name %webout(OPEN) Starts the JSON response %webout(OBJ, work.table) Adds a table, one JSON object per row %webout(ARR, work.table) Adds a table, one JSON array per row (smaller, no column names) %webout(CLOSE) Ends the JSON response

Anything you %put goes into the log, which the caller can ask for with _debug=131 - and which sasjs logcheck fails a deployment on if it contains an error.

docs.title: 2. Put it in the project
docs.text:
sasjs/
├── sasjsconfig.json
├── services/
│   ├── common/
│   │   ├── appinit.sas      <- called first, on app start
│   │   └── getdata.sas
│   └── admin/
│       └── adduser.sas
├── macros/                  <- your macros, folded into the services that use them
└── tests/                   <- one test per service folder

The folders are declared in sasjsconfig.json; subfolders are for organisation and for the SAS 9 / Viya permission model, which grants access per folder. One service per file, lowercase names, and the filename is the service name.

A service is not the only thing a folder can hold: a .js, .py or .r file is compiled and deployed in the same way, which is how a JavaScript or Python backend works. See JavaScript services in the CLI documentation.

docs.title: 3. Compile, build, deploy
docs.text:
Assuming a target is already configured with sasjs add:

sasjs cbd -t myTarget

cbd is compile, build and deploy. Separately:

Command Produces sasjs compile one compiled program per service, macro, with the macros it uses embedded sasjs build the deployable artefact for the target - a Viya service pack, a SAS 9 deployment script, a JSON file tree for SASjs Server sasjs deploy loads that artefact into the environment

What lands, under the target's appLoc:

  • services in /services/<folder>/<name>, as jobs in Viya or stored processes in SAS 9 metadata;
  • tests in /tests/...;
  • jobs in /jobs/... - jobs are compiled without %webout() because they return nothing to a caller.

docs.title: 4. Call it
docs.text:
The adapter does the platform-specific work - authentication, the request shape, reading the response back:

import { SASjs } from '@sasjs/adapter'

const sasjs = new SASjs({
  serverUrl: 'https://sas.example.com',
  appLoc: '/Public/app',
  serverType: 'SASVIYA' // or 'SAS9', or 'SASJS' for SASjs Server
})

const response = await sasjs.request('common/getdata', {
  areas: [{ area: 'Area 1' }]
})

console.log(response.springs) // array of row objects, columns in uppercase

The second argument is the tables to send: each key becomes a WORK table for %webout(FETCH), and each array of objects becomes a CSV the adapter uploads. A table named springs comes back as response.springs, with column names uppercased.

The same call by hand, once you have a token:

curl -s -X POST "https://sas.example.com/SASjsApi/stp/execute?_program=/Public/app/common/getdata&_debug=131" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  --data-urlencode "areas=area
Area 1"

docs.text:
A service with no test is a service that is tested in production. sasjs test runs the project's tests against a target - including a SASjs Server target, where no SAS licence is involved - and reports the results per test:

sasjs test -t myTarget

A test is compiled like a service - %webout() included - and reports PASS or FAIL per row, with coverage of services, jobs and macros in the same result table. See Testing for the test file format and the assertion macros.

docs.title: Why SASjs
docs.text:
SAS is very good at running programs and unusually bad at everything around them. A team that writes excellent SAS still ends up with code that lives on a server, is tested by running it, is deployed by copying files, and is documented in a Word document that is already out of date.

That is not a criticism of the people writing it. SAS tooling has historically been aimed at analysts, not at software delivery, and the delivery part has been left to whoever was available. SASjs is an opinionated answer to that gap.

docs.title: The four symptoms
docs.text:
• The code is not in a repository. It is in SASAUTOS, or in a metadata folder, or on a share that only two people can reach. There is no diff, no review, and no way to know what is deployed where.
  • There is no build. "Deploy" means a person copying files into the right folders in the right order, and remembering the macro library dependency.
  • There is no test. The first execution of a change is the test, and it happens in the environment the business uses.
  • The target is baked in. A program written for a stored process does not run as a Viya job, so a move to Viya means a rewrite of the delivery mechanism even when the logic is unchanged.

docs.title: What SASjs changes
docs.text: Symptom With SASjs Code lives on the server Code lives in git. The server is a deployment target. Deploy is a manual copy sasjs cbd compiles, builds and deploys from the repository, and the same command runs in a pipeline. Tests are manual Services are called from a test harness that runs locally and in CI, with coverage measured. One target per project sasjsconfig.json names targets - Viya, SAS 9, server - and the same project deploys to each. Documentation is a separate document Doxygen headers on macros and services are built into a browsable site by sasjs doc. Style is a matter of opinion Configurable lint rules, enforced in the editor and in the pipeline.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
SASjs has two halves, and they meet at the boundary SAS already has: the macro library runs inside SAS, and the CLI runs outside it.

  1. You write services - .sas files with a header that declares their inputs and outputs. Inside a service you use the macro library: %mf_abort, %mp_jsonout, %ms_getsession, and the rest.
  2. sasjs compile turns each service into a self-contained program, embedding the macros it needs, so the deployed program has no dependency on SASAUTOS and no dependency on the server's file system.
  3. sasjs build writes the artefact a target can consume - a service pack, a Viya job folder, a web app.
  4. sasjs deploy loads it into the environment, using the target's own API: the SASjs web service on SAS 9, the Viya APIs on Viya, the REST API on SASjs Server.
  5. At runtime, a browser or Node application calls the service through the adapter, which knows how to authenticate, how to send tables, and how to read the response - on all three platforms.

Because the compilation step embeds the macros, what runs in production is exactly what was tested, not "the same code, but with whatever is in SASAUTOS this week".

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
• Teams delivering SAS applications - web apps, data-loading tools, reporting portals - where more than one person maintains the code.
  • Teams moving to Viya that want the delivery mechanism to be portable rather than rewritten.
  • SAS shops with a change-control requirement: who changed what, when, and what exactly is deployed.
  • Anyone who has ever debugged production by opening a program in Enterprise Guide over a remote desktop.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text:
• Not a replacement for SAS Studio, Enterprise Guide or SAS DI. Those are development and ETL tools; SASjs is the build and delivery layer underneath what you write in them.
  • Not a scheduler. It deploys jobs; your scheduler still triggers them.
  • Not a metadata manager. It writes to metadata on SAS 9 and to folders on Viya as a deployment act, and leaves governance to the platform.
  • Not a runtime you have to adopt. The macro library is usable without the CLI, the CLI without the adapter, and the adapter against an estate that has never heard of SASjs.

docs.text: Everything in the framework is MIT licensed: the CLI, the adapter, the macro library, the lint rules, the server and the VS Code extension. There is no paid tier and no runtime fee. Commercial support, training and development are available from the team that builds it - see About.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
The reality for many SAS developers is that they are working in locked down windows machines without admin rights. This causes problems when trying to install basic tooling such as GIT or NPM.

The correct approach in such circumstances is to simply make a request for these apps to be installed, so that you can be enabled to create amazing, supportable, maintainable web applications for your end users.

The alternative is to use portable versions that do not require admin privileges to execute.

Note

If you are using powershell, and you don't have access to change your environment variables, you can add your paths to $PROFILE script $env:Path. Thanks Christopher Mortimer for the tip!

  2. Copy the contents to a filesystem location, eg C:\Tools.
  3. Append the path (eg C:\Tools;) to the PATH variable in Environment Variables. You can access the Environment Variables dialog, by right clicking on the Computer > Properties > Advanced system settings > Advanced tab > Environment Variables. If you don’t have permission to access Environment Variables dialog, you can try the following command in the Run dialog: rundll32 sysdm.cpl,EditEnvironmentVariables.

Download the portable .exe file from the releases page and unzip it to a location in your filesystem.

Inside the unzipped folder will be a folder called cmd. This contains the git.exe file. There is also a usr/bin folder - which contains ssh-keygen.exe.

Add both of these locations to the PATH environment variable for your windows account, as per below.

Be sure to hit OK twice for the change to be saved! You can now open a new shell window and create your SSH key using the ssh-keygen command.

docs.text:
• Your own SAS Environment (SAS 9 or Viya).

  • A laptop with a browser, GIT, NPM and VSCodium text editor (or equivalent)

docs.title: System Checks
docs.text: To save time on the day it will help to ensure that you have the above prerequisites. Checks can be made as follows:

docs.title: SAS Access
docs.text: You will need an instance of SAS in order to build the backend!

docs.title: Viya
docs.text:
If you are planning to use Viya, you will also need Admin rights in order to get the API key. You should be able to execute this code without errors: 

options noquotelenmax;
filename mc url "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sasjs/core/main/base/mf_loc.sas";
%inc mc;
data _null_;
  infile "%mf_loc(VIYACONFIG)/etc/SASSecurityCertificateFramework/tokens/consul/default/client.token";
  input token:$64.;
  call symputx('consul_token',token);
run;

It is possible to build apps without admin rights, however you won't be able to auto-deploy using the CLI tool without a client and secret.

You also need the ability to create Job Execution services somewhere in the folder tree. You can check this using /SASJobExecution (or programmatically using SAS Studio).

docs.title: SAS 9
docs.text: You need the ability to create stored processes somewhere in the folder tree. You can check this using SAS Management Console, or DI Studio, or Enterprise Guide (if enabled). You can also try by creating programmatically using SAS Studio.

docs.title: Local Tools
docs.text:
Whilst you could develop on the server, typically builds and changes are made locally and then deployed to a server.

So on your laptop or desktop you will need the following items of software:

docs.title: GIT
docs.text: This is used mainly to clone the seed apps. Install from here: https://git-scm.com/. If you do not have admin rights, try this guide.

docs.title: NPM
docs.text: Node Package Manager (NPM) is a JavaScript framework for managing project dependencies. It also handles installations and a lot of other functionality. It can be downloaded here: https://nodejs.org/en/download. If you do not have admin rights, try this guide.

docs.text: You don't necessarily need VSCode but it's a great editor and includes an integrated terminal for running commands. It can be downloaded (without telemetry) from here: https://vscodium.com/, and a portable version (installable without admin rights) can be obtained from this guide.

Open VScode, select Terminal -> New Terminal, and submit the following commands:

git --version
npm -v
node -v

If you get a version number for each of the above, and the version for node is above 10.3, you're good to go!

docs.title: Components
docs.text: SASjs is "batteries included": six pieces that cover building, running and delivering a SAS application. Each one stands on its own - you can adopt the lint rules without the CLI, or the CLI without the adapter - and they are designed to work together.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
Component Package Runs Does CLI @sasjs/cli Node, terminal or CI Compiles, builds, deploys, tests, lints, documents Macro Core @sasjs/core Inside SAS The macros services are written with Adapter @sasjs/adapter Browser or Node Talks to SAS from JavaScript Server @sasjs/server Node + a SAS binary A REST API, drive and app portal on Foundation SAS Lint @sasjs/lint Node, editor SAS code-quality rules VS Code extension Editor Highlighting, lint, execution, build and deploy

  • CLI

    create, compile, build, deploy, test, lint, doc - the project, from the terminal or a pipeline.

  • Macro Core

    About 200 SAS macros: JSON output, table transfer, metadata, file operations, error handling.

  • Adapter

    One JavaScript API for Viya, SAS 9 and server: auth, service calls, tables, files, streamed apps.

  • Server

    An open-source web server on the SAS binary - a REST API, a drive, and an app portal.

  • Lint

    Configurable code-quality rules, in the editor and in CI, from one .sasjslint.

  • VS Code

    Highlighting, lint diagnostics, execution and the build commands, in the editor.

docs.title: How they fit together
docs.text:
your service (.sas)  +  macro core  ->  sasjs compile  ->  compiled program
                                                                   |
                        sasjs build  ->  artefact per target  <----+
                                                                   |
   sasjs deploy  ->  Viya jobs  |  SAS 9 stored processes  |  SASjs Server drive
                                                                   |
   browser / Node app  -- adapter -->  the deployed service  <------+

The compiler embeds the macros a service uses, so the program that runs in production carries its own dependencies at the version that was reviewed - there is no SASAUTOS on the server to disagree with the repository.

The next step depends on what you are building: services for a backend called from a browser, React or Angular for a full application, or Backend SAS for a delivery pipeline.

docs.title: Adapter
docs.text:
The JavaScript library that connects a front end to SAS. It exists because the request that runs a job, the login, and the shape of the response are different on every platform - and the application code should not be.

npm install @sasjs/adapter

import { SASjs } from '@sasjs/adapter'

const sasjs = new SASjs({
  serverUrl: 'https://sas.example.com',
  appLoc: '/Public/app/my-project',
  serverType: 'SASVIYA' // 'SAS9', or 'SASJS' for SASjs Server
})

const res = await sasjs.request('common/getdata', { areas: [{ area: 'Area 1' }] })

docs.title: What it handles
docs.text:
• Authentication - the Viya token exchange, the SAS 9 stored process login, and the SASjs Server token model, behind one login call.
  • Service calls - request() runs a service and resolves with the tables it returned, column names uppercased, whichever platform served it.
  • Tables in - an array in the request payload becomes a CSV the server turns into a WORK table, which is how a browser sends data to %webout(FETCH).
  • Files - upload to the server's drive, and download from it.
  • Streamed web apps - fetching the index and the assets of an application that SAS itself is serving.
  • Compute vs JES - on Viya, either the Job Execution Service or the compute APIs directly, which is what a Node process needs.

docs.title: The classes
docs.text:
Export For SASjs the one you normally use: config, login, request(), files, and the platform-specific clients underneath SASViyaApiClient the Viya REST APIs directly - contexts, sessions, jobs, files SAS9ApiClient the SAS 9 stored process web service SASjsApiClient the SASjs Server REST API

The seed applications use SASjs and nothing else; the lower-level clients are there for a Node process that needs a specific API rather than a service call.

docs.title: Where it is used
docs.text: Every SASjs front end is built on it: the React and Angular seed apps, Data Controller for SAS, and the CLI itself, which uses the Node build of the same library to deploy and to run code remotely.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Documentation - the API, the config, and the platform differences.
  • Source and releases, and @sasjs/adapter on npm.
  • React or Angular - an application that uses it.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
The command line tool that turns a folder of SAS files into something deployed. It owns the project config, the compile step, the artefacts, the deploy to each platform, the test harness, the linter and the documentation generator.

npm i -g @sasjs/cli
sasjs --help

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: Command For create scaffolds a project - plain, or from the react, angular, minimal, sasonly or jobs template add defines a target: where it deploys, and the credentials it uses compile one program per service, with the macros it uses embedded build the deployable artefact for a target - a Viya service pack, a SAS 9 script, a SASjs Server file tree deploy loads that artefact into the environment cbd compile, build and deploy in one step test runs the project's tests, with coverage, returning JSON, JUnit XML, LCOV or CSV lint configurable SAS code-quality rules, before the commit rather than after the incident logcheck reads a SAS log and fails on what SAS printed - the run that reported success and logged ERROR 22-322 doc generates HTML documentation from the doxygen headers in your macros and services run executes a SAS program in a compute or workspace session job executes a job that is already deployed, and brings back its log and output flow runs a set of jobs in dependency order, on Viya or SASjs Server request calls a deployed service, and writes the response to a file fs lists, uploads and downloads files on the server's drive web packages a front end as streaming SAS services auth, context, folder, db, servicepack, snippets, version the supporting operations of a deployment

docs.title: One project, three platforms
docs.text:
A target decides where a project goes: SASVIYA, SAS9 or SASJS (SASjs Server). The same sasjs cbd -t <target> deploys to any of them, and a project can carry a target for each - which is how the same code is tested against a local server and delivered to production.

sasjs add                 # a target, with prompts for its connection details
sasjs cbd -t viya         # compile, build, deploy
sasjs cb                  # the artefact, without the deploy

docs.title: In a pipeline
docs.text:
Nothing about the CLI assumes a human at the keyboard: sasjs cbd and sasjs test exit non-zero on failure, logs are written to sasjsresults, and sasjs logcheck turns a SAS log into a pass or fail. That is the whole of the CI integration - no plugin, no server.

sasjs cbd -t myTarget && sasjs test -t myTarget && sasjs logcheck

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:

  • Services - the first end-to-end walkthrough.
  • Backend SAS - project layout and targets.
  • Source and releases.

docs.title: Macro Core
docs.text:
The runtime half of the framework: about 200 SAS macros for building applications, plus the plumbing the rest of SASjs depends on. It is a normal SASAUTOS library - usable on its own, without the CLI, the adapter or anything else.

/* the whole library, in one file, without touching the server */
filename mc url "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sasjs/core/main/all.sas";
%inc mc;

/* or from npm, at a version you pin */
/* npm install @sasjs/core --save-dev */

docs.title: What is in it
docs.text:
Folder What it covers base/ the general library: JSON and CSV output (mp_jsonout), table transfer, file and folder operations, error handling (mf_abort), hashing, encoding, dates and strings meta/ SAS 9 metadata: users, groups, libraries, folders, stored processes, and the web service plumbing metax/ metadata helpers built on the metadata data step functions (mmx_) fcmp/ functions for use inside proc fcmp (mcf_) ddl/ table DDL generation (mddl_)

Naming is by prefix: mf_ for functions, mp_ for programs and output, mm_ for metadata, mmx_ for the metadata data step functions, mcf_ for proc fcmp functions, mddl_ for DDL.

docs.title: Why it matters to the framework
docs.text:
sasjs compile embeds the macros a service uses into the compiled program. That is what makes a deployed service independent of SASAUTOS on the server and of the server's file system - the program that runs in production carries its own dependencies, at the version that was reviewed.

%webout(), which every service and test uses to return data, is generated by the compiler from this library.

docs.title: Using it directly
docs.text:
The library is useful without the CLI:

%inc "path/to/core/all.sas";

%mf_abort(iftrue=(&syscc ne 0), msg=Something went wrong upstream)

%mp_jsonout(OPEN, jref=_webout)
%mp_jsonout(OBJ, work.results)
%mp_jsonout(CLOSE, jref=_webout)

Every macro carries a doxygen header with its parameters and an example, and the documentation site is generated from those headers.

docs.title: Lint
docs.text:
A SAS code-quality checker. Rules are declarative and configurable, results carry line and column, and the same config drives the CLI and the editor - so the argument about style happens once, in a file, rather than in every pull request.

sasjs lint          # from a project with a .sasjslint

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text:
The rules cover the things that actually cost a SAS team time:

  • structure - a header on every file and every macro, %mend naming its macro, macro parameters in parentheses, no nested comments in a doxygen header;
  • hygiene - no hardcoded filerefs, no non-local macro variables leaking scope, one macro per file, the filename matching the macro name;
  • formatting - indentation, trailing spaces, line length, invisible characters, tabs;
  • safety - banned strings, discouraged functions, %abort where a silent failure would be worse.

A rule is switched on in .sasjslint by naming it - a boolean, or a number where it takes a value - and its severity is set separately:

{
  "hasDoxygenHeader": true,
  "noTrailingSpaces": true,
  "maxLineLength": 300,
  "indentationMultiple": 2,
  "severityLevel": {
    "hasDoxygenHeader": "error",
    "maxLineLength": "warn"
  },
  "ignoredMacros": ["webout", "mpeinit"]
}

A rule left out is off. maxLineLength at 0 is also off, which is how a single rule is disabled in a project that inherits the rest.

docs.title: Where it runs
docs.text:
• In the CLI - sasjs lint for a folder or a whole project, with an exit code a pipeline can act on; sasjs lint fix applies the fixes that are mechanical, and sasjs lint init writes a starting config.
  • In VS Code - diagnostics as you type, from the same config, through the SASjs extension.
  • In sasjs compile - a service is compiled the same way whether or not it was linted, so lint is a deliberate step rather than a silent gate.

docs.title: The rule set is a shared asset
docs.text: The rules that ship with the tool are the ones the SASjs libraries themselves are held to - @sasjs/core, the CLI, the adapter and the server all lint in CI. Adopting the tool means adopting a rule set that has been argued about once, in public, in a config file.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:

  • CLI reference for sasjs lint.
  • VS Code extension - the same rules in the editor.

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
An open-source web server wrapped around the SAS binary. It gives an estate with Foundation SAS - or a laptop - somewhere to deploy to, with the same project that deploys to Viya: a REST API, a drive for files and services, and a portal for applications.

linux.zip  ->  ./api-linux     # a single binary, no Node install required

docs.title: What it provides
docs.text: REST API stored programs from a URL, sessions with state, log and output, and a Swagger reference served by the server itself SASjs Drive a file system for services, apps and data, addressed over the same API - this is what sasjs deploy writes to Stored programs a program is a file on the drive; the extension decides the runtime App portal uploaded web applications, launched by users, with per-user and per-group permissions Runtimes SAS, JavaScript, Python and R, chosen per program

docs.title: Two modes
docs.text:
• Desktop - single user, no authentication, no database. This is how a developer runs a backend locally, or how a demo runs without a SAS licence for the web tier.
  • Server - multi-user, authenticated, with a database for users and permissions, LDAP or OpenID Connect for identity, and the same API underneath.

docs.title: Why it exists
docs.text:
A SASjs project targets SASVIYA, SAS9 or SASJS. The third is this server: it means a project can be developed, tested and demonstrated with no Viya estate and no metadata server, and it means SAS 9 shops have a way to run web applications without the stored process web tier in the path.

The JavaScript runtime is also how a service can have a mock backend: the same services, a different implementation, no SAS at all.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Documentation - installation, settings, sessions, stored programs and the API.
  • Source and releases, and @sasjs/server on npm.
  • Deploying to Viya - the same deployment model, on Viya.

docs.title: VS Code extension
docs.text:
SAS development in VS Code, with the framework's tooling inside it: syntax highlighting for SAS, lint results as you type, execution of a program against a real server, and the CLI's commands without switching to a terminal.

Install it from the VS Code Marketplace or from Open VSX.

docs.title: What it adds
docs.text: Feature Detail Syntax highlighting SAS language support - DATA step, macros, PROC SQL, and the doxygen headers the framework uses Linting the SASjs Lint rules, as you type, from .sasjslint Execution run a program against Viya, SAS 9 or SASjs Server, and read the log in the output pane Build and deploy compile, build, deploy and cbd for a target, from the command palette Formatting the formatter's output applied to the open file

docs.title: Why it is part of the framework
docs.text: The extension is not a separate product with its own idea of a project: it reads the same sasjs/sasjsconfig.json, calls the same CLI, and reports the same lint rules. A developer who works in VS Code and a pipeline that deploys from a container are running the same commands against the same config.
